To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

T cell receptor gene (TCR) gene rearrangements are present in more than ninety per cent of childhood precursor B cell ALL, and that the majority of TCR gene rearrangements can be used for minimal residual disease monitoring.
TCRB gene deletions are the most common T cell receptor gene abnormalities in precursor B ALL and that TCRD and/or TCRG gene targets are available in 80% of cases for MRD monitoring.

TCRB, -D and -G genes are frequently rearranged and deleted in precursor B ALL, that heteroduplex TCRG and -D analysis can be used to identify PCR targets for detection and monitoring of MRD in precursor B ALL patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of clonotypic TCRG and IGHV gene rearrangements for MRD monitoring in childhood precursor B ALL.
the identification of alternative PCR targets for MRD monitoring in precursor B ALL.
a comprehensive analysis of TCR gene rearrangements as a tool to improve the detection of minimal residual leukemia in precursor B ALL.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the T cell receptor gene locus analysis is of great clinical relevance for childhood precursor B ALL.
TCRB gene analysis should be used for MRD monitoring in approximately 35% of patients and that TCRG and/ or TCRD analysis should be performed in the remaining 65% of patients.
in 93% of childhood precursor ALL cases one or more clonal TCR genes are involved in the leukemic process and in 55% of cases two or three clonal TCR gene rearrangements can be identified.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TCRG gene analysis is more suitable than TCRD analysis for the detection of MRD in childhood precursor B cell ALL.
in more than 80% of precursor B ALL patients, one or more TCRG and or TCRD genes are rearranged and/or are deleted.

TCRB and TCRD rearrangements are less frequent in childhood precursor B ALL (35% and 55%, respectively) compared to TCRG gene (59%), but that in 93% of patients at least one gene rearrangement is detectable, which can be used for MRD studies in the majority of patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the T cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement status of precursor B cell acute leukemia is much more common and complex than previously recognized and that the TCRB, -D, -G genes are potential PCR-based targets for detection of MRD in the vast majority of precursor B cell ALL patients.
T cell receptor gene analysis is a powerful tool for detection of MRD and can be applied to a majority of precursor B ALL patients.
MRD studies with TCRG or TCRD genes should be considered as an alternative to IGH studies in the majority of childhood ALL patients.
